title: What To Say To Build Rapport With Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Building on his broader principle of being consistently pleasant to build rapport, Linsin offers three guidelines for the moment a student actually approaches to talk. First, listen: let the student fully guide the conversation with no ulterior motive of steering it toward behavior or academics, since genuinely listening to kids is rare among adults and builds outsized influence. Second, be real: he criticizes teachers who overact with exaggerated enthusiasm and warns it comes across as a turn-off even to young students, recommending a relaxed, matter-of-fact, even 'kindly gruff' authenticity instead. Third, be honest: while maintaining professional boundaries about what not to share, a teacher should otherwise tell the truth plainly, since inauthenticity breeds distrust, especially with students who've experienced manipulation and false praise before. He closes by arguing students always sense whether a teacher genuinely likes them, and that this unspoken signal determines whether real trust and influence are possible.
points: When a student approaches to talk, let them fully guide the conversation and respond only with light, curious questions — no ulterior motive toward behavior or academics.
Avoid overacting rapport with exaggerated smiles and enthusiasm; a relaxed, matter-of-fact, even 'kindly gruff' authenticity works better, even with young students.
Be honest about personal opinions (say so if you don't like video games or soccer) while still maintaining professional boundaries about what you won't reveal.
Inauthenticity breeds distrust, especially in students who've already experienced manipulation, false praise, or flattery from adults.
Students always sense, even unconsciously, whether a teacher genuinely likes them, and that unspoken signal determines whether real trust and influence are possible.
quotes: By taking on an easygoing, good-humored disposition, your students will come to you and want to get to know you better.
Always let the student guide the conversation. Be a backboard and respond to them by asking light questions. Be curious and open and they will talk and talk.
Few adults actually listen to kids. So when you do, your likability and sway will soar.
Stop trying to please or sell your students on anything. Instead, relax. Be matter-of-fact. You can even be kindly gruff.
Inauthenticity causes distrust. This is especially so with challenging students who’ve been subject to near-constant manipulation, false praise, and flattery.
Your students will always know whether you like them or not. It’s something you can’t hide.
